opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is that the main lever has shifted from pre-training to what happens after it, and especially to reinforcement learning with verifiable feedback.

For a few years the recipe was fairly simple. You collected more data, built a bigger model, used more compute, and intelligence kind of emerged from next-token prediction. That still matters a lot. Pre-training gives you the foundation, the world knowledge, the raw capacity. But we've started to feel the limits. High-quality human text isn't infinite, and simply scaling up doesn't give you the same returns on reasoning that it once did.

What changed is that people realized the model can learn from its own attempts. If you give it problems where the answer can be checked, like math, code, or tasks with clear success criteria, and you let it think longer, try things, and get rewarded when it's right, it starts to develop behaviors nobody explicitly taught it. It learns to reflect, to backtrack, to verify its own steps. To me that was a very striking moment. It felt less like teaching the model answers and more like creating an environment where it could discover how to reason.

So the question has moved from "how do we feed the model more data" to "how do we design the right environments and reward signals." That's a very different way of thinking. Compute is spent at inference time too, not just during training. And the bottleneck becomes things like: how do you get reliable rewards for tasks that are harder to verify, like writing, research, or long-horizon agent work? How do you keep the model from gaming the reward?

I'd also say the field has become more of an engineering and systems discipline. A lot of progress comes from the details: data quality, training stability, infrastructure efficiency. Teams that are disciplined about those details can do surprisingly well even without the biggest budgets, which I think is very healthy for the field.

So in one sentence: we went from imitation to exploration. The model used to mostly learn to imitate humans, and now it's increasingly learning by trying things itself. I think that's where a lot of the next leaps in intelligence will come from.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that we've moved from asking "how much knowledge can we pour into the model" to asking "how do we let the model learn from its own experience."

For a long time, the whole game was pretraining. You scraped more data, you scaled up parameters, you scaled up compute, and intelligence came almost as a byproduct of compression. The scaling laws told you roughly what you'd get. That paradigm hasn't disappeared, but it has run into a very practical wall: high-quality human text is finite. We're close to having used the internet.

So the center of gravity shifted to post-training, and specifically to reinforcement learning. The question became: given a model that already has a strong prior, how do you give it an environment and a signal so it can get better by trying things? Math and code were the first places this worked, because you have a verifier. The answer is right or wrong, the tests pass or they don't. The model generates many attempts, the correct ones get reinforced, and you see things like long chains of reasoning emerge without anyone hand-writing them. That was a real surprise to many of us, how little supervision was actually needed once the reward was clean.

What I find most interesting is that this changes what "data" means. Previously, data was something humans produced and we consumed. Now the model produces its own trajectories, and the scarce resource is no longer text, it's good environments and good reward signals. The people building the best models today are spending enormous effort on that, on building tasks where the model can act, get feedback, and be judged reliably.

The open problem, and I think the next big change, is extending this beyond domains with easy verification. Writing, research, open-ended agentic work, these don't have a clean checker. So you're seeing a lot of work on learned reward models, on self-evaluation, on using the model to critique the model. If we solve that, the ceiling moves a lot. If we don't, we'll have systems that are superhuman at competition math and still mediocre at judgment.

So in one sentence: the biggest change is that intelligence is increasingly coming from the model's interaction with the world rather than from memorizing what humans already wrote.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that we’re moving from treating intelligence mainly as a matter of scale to asking how a model learns to solve problems. For a long time, the approach was to use more data, build a bigger model, and invest more compute in training. That remains important, but now there’s much more attention on what happens after that initial training: how the model learns from feedback, checks its work, and spends more time reasoning through a difficult question.

That also changes what we mean by improvement. A model can sound very fluent and still fail to solve the problem. The goal is to make it more reliable at reaching a useful answer, especially when the task requires several steps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that we’re moving from scaling pretraining alone to also scaling how models learn to reason. Before, much of the progress came from training larger models on more data. Now, reinforcement learning and computation at inference time are becoming increasingly important: giving a model room to explore an approach, check its work, and correct mistakes before answering.

That changes what we focus on as researchers. It’s no longer just, “How much knowledge can the model absorb?” It’s also, “How can it learn to use that knowledge to solve a problem it hasn’t seen before?”
